title: Optimize Walkthrough: cache-hit lifecycle & batching playbook - Orbit Analytics
summary: Redwood AE/SE walked Orbit through an Optimize-focused demo covering batching strategies, KV/prefix cache lifecycle, TTL heuristics, and a simple cost model simulation. Customer is evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs VPC/private for a sessionized Q&A product; main concerns are tail latency, data residency, and predictable unit cost. Next steps: share cost spreadsheet, run a 1-week sandbox with sample traffic, and provide SOC2 + KMS notes.
topics: Cost model walkthrough and sensitivity by concurrency
Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private deployment tradeoffs

Liam: Provide 48-hour representative trace sample and P95 latency SLA target by 2026-09-05
next_steps: Schedule a 1-week sandbox run with 50k daily sessions (tentative start 2026-09-07)
Agree on pilot success criteria (P95 < 400ms, cost per 1k tokens < $X)

transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-09-01 16:00 PDT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Devon Patel (Redwood SE), Liam Garcia (Orbit Head of ML), Priya Nair (Orbit Eng Manager), Owen Brooks (SRE)
Shared links: Optimize playbook deck (drive link), cost spreadsheet (to be uploaded), SOC2 + KMS notes (will send)
---
00:00 Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um, we'll do a quick 50-minute walkthrough, we'll focus on batching and cache recommendations for your sessionized q&a flow. Devon will drive the console demo.
00:18 Liam: sounds good, yeah, excited to see the concrete numbers. quick context, we have many short sessions, average prompt length 120 tokens, responses about 300 tokens, and we do session continuation with user context - so lots of KV hits early on.
00:32 Devon: perfect, that matches some of the profiling we requested. quick question, are you persisting session state in your app or doing it via the model side?
00:44 Priya: we're storing a compact conversation state server-side and sending a session id. we want Redwood to handle the KV cache so we don't send full context every time.
00:58 Owen: and security wise, we'll need VPC or a private deployment later; initial pilot can be hosted if data is redacted.
01:08 Maya: yup, typical. ok, high level first: batching reduces per-token cost but can add tail latency; caching (prefix / KV) reduces compute per request when you get a cache hit. the goal of today's playbook is to show thresholds and TTL heuristics that hit your cost + latency targets.
01:26 Devon: jumping into the console — note: some of the screenshots in the deck might say 'Redwood Optimizer' in auto-caption, that's our internal label, but product is Redwood Optimize.
01:35 02:03 Devon: [screen share start] so here's the Optimize panel. first card is 'batching policy recommendation' — we can tune target batch size, max wait ms, and concurrency buckets. for your profile I'd suggest start with target batch 16, max wait 30ms for p10-focused apps, or target 8 and 10ms wait if you need tighter p99.
02:25 Priya: when you say 'max wait 30ms' does that mean requests sit on an internal queue for up to 30ms waiting to fill a batch?
02:33 Devon: exactly, yeah. so average added latency is roughly wait/(batch size) but there's variability; for throughput sims we model arrival distribution.
02:43 Liam: our biggest pain is p95 spikes during morning traffic. we care most about p95/p99 not average.
02:51 Devon: noted. for p95 stability we usually do two things: keep target batch smaller (8-12) and enable latency-aware routing that falls back to a smaller model variant if queue builds.
03:02 Maya: also prefix/KV cache helps a lot for sessionized queries — if user asks follow-ups, the cache returns K/V outputs for prefixes and avoids re-decoding earlier tokens.
03:12 Owen: is that the same as session cache? what's prefix vs session?
03:18 Devon: good question — in our terminology: prefix cache stores KV state keyed by deterministic prefix (e.g., system + first user message). session cache ties to a session id and can be warmed as the conversation evolves. prefix cache is higher hit-rate for replicated opening prompts, session cache is higher hit for continuing flows.
03:33 Priya: hmm, in our product we have a standard initial prompt template that 80% of sessions use, so prefix cache seems promising.
03:41 Devon: exactly — we ran a sim for a similar customer and saw 30-45% token reduction with prefix caching alone. combined with batching you get multiplicative savings.
03:52 04:15 Liam: show us the cost model simulation, please.
04:21 Devon: sure, opening the cost sim tool — input: avg input 120 tokens, avg output 300, sessions per day 50k, concurrency 120. baseline: no cache, batching conservative (4), hosted model A -> unit cost X.
04:36 Devon: huh, I'm going to toggle a TTL heuristic: short-lived prefix TTL of 1h vs a long TTL of 6h, and enable session affinity for 75% of traffic to keep same inference worker.
04:50 Devon: with 1h TTL we see 22% token reduction, estimated cost reduction 18% at your traffic. with 6h TTL it's 34% token reduction, cost reduction ~28% but memory footprint increases for cache K/V store.
05:05 Priya: memory footprint meaning what? if we host with Redwood, where does the cache reside?
05:11 Devon: good, so hosted: cache is on the serving plane, managed by Redwood. Dedicated/Private: cache can be local to customer's reserved pool or plumbed into your VPC-attached Redis if you prefer. the memory increases linearly with active unique prefixes; our console shows estimated GBs required.
05:28 Owen: can we set an eviction policy based on recency or freq? we don't want stale stuff for long TTLs.
05:34 Devon: yes — console supports LRU frequency-boosted eviction and an adaptive TTL: items degrade to a shorter effective TTL after N accesses. this reduces long tail memory while preserving hot keys.
05:45 Liam: what's N typically?
05:46 Devon: default N=3 hits in 30 minutes for hot promotion. but you can tune to your workload; during the sandbox we can profile and auto-suggest values.
05:58 06:10 Priya: about concurrency — you mentioned session affinity. how does affinity affect batching? I imagine affinity reduces potential batch sizes?
06:20 Devon: tradeoff. affinity keeps requests on the same worker which helps KV cache hit rate (since KV is local), but if too sticky, you reduce opportunities to coalesce requests into larger batches across workers. we use an affinity window — e.g., 200ms where repeated requests go to same worker; beyond that we allow rebalancing.
06:37 Maya: for your profile with many short sessions, a hybrid: prefix cache on global layer + 200ms affinity for active sessions gives good hit rate without sacrificing batching too much.
06:46 Liam: can we do a numerical example? say concurrency 120, arrival distribution bursty with peak 600 RPS, how will batching look?
06:57 Devon: yes. with target batch 12 and max wait 30ms, on steady 120 concurrency you average batch 9. during 600 RPS bursts you'd hit bigger batches, sometimes up to 20 which increases throughput but could push p99 unless we cap max batch size or fallback route. we can show the sim charts — I'll export one.
07:23 Priya: and routing fallback — you mentioned smaller model variant. do you automatically degrade model size to keep latency?
07:31 Devon: we support policy-based routing. you can set SLOs and a fallback model family. e.g., if expected p95 > 350ms, route to a quantized variant or smaller architecture. the console sim shows expected quality regression; that's where Redwood Optimize integrates with your evals to check if fallbacks are acceptable.
07:48 Liam: about quality — how do you detect when fallback is degrading user experience vs acceptable variance?
07:54 Devon: integration with our eval runs: you provide a prompt set, we run A/B style comparison and flag regressions by metric (ROUGE / embedding similarity / task-specific metric). you can tie regression alerts to auto rollback.
08:08 Owen: concerning security and data retention, if cache is managed by Redwood, what's the retention policy and encryption?
08:15 Maya: we encrypt data at rest using KMS, optionally bring-your-own key. retention is configurable; for hosted we recommend TTLs aligned with your compliance needs, and we keep audit logs of evictions and accesses. we'll send the SOC2 + KMS slide deck after.
08:28 Liam: ok. show us a sample cost comparison: hosted vs dedicated vs private for our baseline traffic.
08:34 Devon: pulling up the quick cost matrix - baseline (no cache) hosted $A/day, dedicated with reserved 8xA100 equivalent pool with 20% utilization is $B/day flat plus infra, private has higher up-front license but gives lowest variable token expense. once you add prefix cache with 34% token savings, hosted goes down to ~0.72*A, dedicated is more efficient at high sustained throughput.
08:54 Priya: so for pilot, hosted seems easiest; for production we might move to dedicated if sustained.
09:00 Maya: exactly, many customers start hosted to iterate and switch to dedicated when they hit predictable QPS. the Optimize console supports the same config artifacts across modes so rollout is smooth.
09:10 09:30 Devon: quick demo of the cache heatmap — here we can see key cardinality over time and a predicted eviction pressure. your sample trace (we loaded a synthetic one) shows 68% of keys are cold after 24 hours; that suggests 6h TTL is sufficient for most active sessions but 24h is overkill.
09:47 Liam: what's causing cold keys? is it one-off users?
09:50 Devon: yes, ephemeral sessions from casual users. the heatmap helps set a split TTL: short TTL for cold, long for frequently reused prefixes.
10:02 Priya: can we pipeline TTL tiers automatically? like auto-promote hot keys to long TTL and demote when cold?
10:10 Devon: yes, that's the adaptive TTL I mentioned — auto-promote after threshold hits. console shows settings under Cache Policies.
10:18 Owen: any impact on billing if cache memory grows? we worry about unbounded cost surprises.
10:26 Devon: for hosted we present memory estimate and a capped billing model — you can set an upper memory cap and we can overflow to a lower-cost backing store or evict aggressively. dedicated/private you manage memory in your reserved pool. billing transparency is in Optimize -> Cost Simulation.
10:42 Liam: you had an earlier number showing 30-45% savings with prefix cache — can you explain the delta between 22% and 34% we saw in the sim?
10:52 Devon: differences come from two axes: TTL and session reuse. 22% was conservative 1h TTL; 34% used 6h TTL + session affinity + slightly larger batch sizes. also traffic skew matters—if your sessions reuse initial prompts a lot, prefix cache is higher.
11:07 Maya: also note that some words in the transcript may show 'K-V cache' — K/V is the internal representation of key/value attention state. sometimes transcription calls it 'kayvee cache' in the recording.
11:18 11:40 Liam: ok this is helpful. a question about model compilation/quantization and cache compatibility: if you quantize a model variant, does cache from full precision still apply?
11:50 Devon: cache stores keys at the latent KV level not raw tokens, so when switching between variants you need architecture-compatible variants to reuse cache. quantized variants that are architecture-identical typically can reuse the same KV shapes, but cross-architecture caches don't transfer. console flags compatibility and suggests compatible fallback families.
12:08 Priya: what's the rollout path for canarying cache changes? we don't want to break production.
12:15 Devon: there's a canary policy in Optimize: you can enable cache policy change for X% of traffic, monitor quality/regressions and memory pressure, then full roll out. we keep a fallback to previous cache epoch.
12:27 Owen: for the sandbox run, can Redwood capture traces and give us a delta report? like tokens saved, p95 improvements?
12:33 Devon: yes, sandbox telemetry includes a Delta report with token delta, latency distribution, and cost delta by day. we'll include a daily dashboard.
12:41 Liam: timing wise, if we start 2026-09-07 pilot how quickly can you turn up the sandbox?
12:46 Maya: SE can spin sandbox in 24-48 hours after we get the trace and service account. full instrumentation within 72 hours.
12:52 Maya: okay real quick, I'm going to read out the recap and action items: Devon will upload the cost-by-concurrency CSV and a sample sim export; I'll send SOC2 + KMS notes and enterprise pricing; Liam to share a 48-hour trace; tentative sandbox start 2026-09-07. any changes?
13:08 Liam: sounds right. also please include a short note on fallback model quality metrics so our PMs can review.
13:14 Devon: will do — I'll include the eval summary and example A/B outputs.
13:20 Priya: one last question - do you support bringing your own Redis as the KV store? we prefer to manage state for private deployments.
13:26 Devon: yes — private/dedicated can plumb to your managed Redis or a network-attached cache. hosted gives managed cache; for BYO we provide connectors and recommended network configs (VPC peering + IAM).
13:36 Owen: awesome. that's it from ops.
13:38 Maya: great. we'll send notes by EOD tomorrow and the spreadsheets by Friday. thanks everyone.
13:45 Liam: thanks. good demo.
13:48 [call end]
